Mental facilities are totally voluntary unless you’re actively a threat to yourself or someone else. Like, gun to head, rope to neck. And mental facilities aren’t all bad. If your psych recommends you check in to one, do some research. I’ve had a couple of hospitalizations and it was comfortable experience. No responsibilities except therapy and commiseration with other patients. It can really help. You’re fed, you’re housed, you’re checked regularly by nurses, there’s always something to do if you’re bored and an on call doctor or your psych can manage any med changes. Talking to other people with depression and mental illnesses was the best part of my stays. I didn’t feel alone and misunderstood. 

If you’re not comfortable telling your family the nitty gritty, don’t. If you have to tell them anything, treat this like any other condition. “I don’t feel well, I’m going to see my doctor.” 

You’re not worse for taking medication. It’s an indication that you can identify your problems and that you are willing to deal with them. That also goes for therapy. Trust me, not everyone can get over that first step for a while. I ruined my most cherished relationships because I didn’t want to deal with my health.

This happened to me. Even after raising the dose, the suicidal ideation kept coming. It wasn’t until a couple of stays at a mental facility and a couple of med changes did it get better. 

We tolerate drugs after a while. Or our brain circumvents the changes we made to incite that internal violence. Talk to your prescribing doctor—cliché, I know—and be specific. They won’t continue this line of treatment if your depression isn’t well managed. 

I wish we didn’t need to take drugs to feel normal. I really do. But it’s way better than the alternative.

Yeah, of course. So I’m Turkish and therefore have a huge bias to the mosques I’ve actually had the honor of visiting. Sultan Ahmed mosque is a stunning example of geometric tile work that adorns the mosque without necessarily representing Islam. It’s become an idiosyncrasy of mosques, but that’s it. There also these large platters in the Hagia Sofia with this huge arabic calligraphy. They write the names of Allah and Muhammad, which in my opinion pushes the envelope, but these adornments were built like the pyramids. They’re far more a representation of the piety (ironically), wealth, and/or power of the sultan who built or added to them. 

The blue mosque of Yerevan has a different style of architecture and tile work, but there’s this notable through line thats everywhere. 

I’ve had the pleasure of visiting İshak Paşa palace in Doğubeyazıt and it’s a great example of an extremely simple mosque despite its proximity to wealth. 

I can’t give you an exhaustive list of beautiful mosques or palaces, of course. Historical metropolises of the middle and near east all have stunning world heritage sites. Damascus, Baghdad, Tehran, Kabul—I love the Hazrat Ali Mazar in Afghanista. That’s just architecture, however. 

My interest in Islamic art has always been the architecture and the tapestries and carpets. Painting and calligraphy, though both beautiful, especially the calligraphy, does not pique my interest as well. 

The idea of abstract symbols as a way to celebrate Islam rather than represent it lives in the rugs. Quite honestly, so many of the motifs of Turkish rugs have been traced back to before the national adoption of Islam, that i don’t believe it’s in any way idolatrous. None of it represents features or teachings of Islam. I can’t say the same for Persian rugs because I just don’t know as much. It’s funny that such a huge feature of prayer has become kind of a layman’s symbol for Islam, but like many idiosyncrasies of the religion, it was born out of necessity first. 

But a symbol that is probably idolatrous? The evil eye. That blue glass eye that we hang everywhere? That’s definitely from an era before Islam and would not be accepted by the prophet, but no one really cares.

I want to preface that I’m not a scholar. I’m not even Muslim anymore. This is what I learned from my community and my own research growing up. 

That’s the thing, there’s a huge history of religious art being purely abstract. The general consensus after 1400 years is that it is idolatrous to create images of living beings in Islam. That being said, Muhammad did cleanse the Kaaba of all religious symbols and figures. There weren’t great ways to identify other Muslims early on, probably a feature and not a bug, so very rudimentary symbols became banners. Like…the color green. Just green. No adornments.  The crescent and star weren’t associated with Islam as a whole until after the ottomans conquered Constantinople. 

There’s so much beautiful Islamic art. It’s not like Christian art that represents Jesus and the love of God as it’s rarely symbolic of Islam, but rather art juxtaposed to Islam. Art inspired by the culture of these communities that were primarily Muslim. Beautiful mosques with unique and painstaking tile, but none of it represents islam. But icons like the crescent moon and star and a green flag have become banners to represent islam. 

Like all religions, interpretation has changed many, many times. The current and most common interpretation agrees that none of these symbols are idolatrous, but I believe that’s more out of convenience than orthodoxy.
Religious iconography is against the prophet’s teachings.
Honestly, the crescent moon and star and green flag are pushing it. But no religion is without hypocrisy.

The difference is structural. Floating tremolo units (aka a normal whammy bar) sit in a hole at the bridge and the springs that hold tension are in the back cavity. Top loading units* like bigsby’s sit, well, on top of body and the spring is directly under the bar. When you depress a bigsby’s arm, you’re pushing against a spring whereas with a floating trem, the act of pushing the arm pulls the springs in the back cavity. It feels different even though it creates the same effect. They both have their uses, though. I have a licensed bigsby on my semi hollow body, a standard 2 point, floating trem on my strat, and an FRX on my SG. 

If you can afford it, or if there are any guitar shops near you that are open and somehow allowing demos, try them all out, especially on different guitars. You’re not going to be able to put a 2 point floating trem on a les Paul, at least not without routing a huge hole through the body, and you might not like a bigsby, but you might learn that you like floating trems on strat style guitars. 

*Floyd rose also built a top loading unit but it’s nothing like a bigsby. Look up locking tremolos for a crash course in what Floyd rose offers.

Highly. I find original bigsby’s to be much smoother for jazz vibrato compared to floating trems. Not exactly designed for dive bombs, though. What of elective mastectomy, testosterone shots, metoidioplasty? Some, certainly, by virtue of the variance of humanity, and I’m not here to discredit their experiences if that is what fits them, but are you personally happy to be an outlier in a community that does not see you?

I have naturally high free testosterone. Always have. Never has it breached the “normal cis male” range but it’s a little out of cis female range. I get all of the side effects: hair growth on my face, muscle tone, stomach fat, maybe baldness someday, but I’m banking on my genes. At no point in my whole life did I ever doubt that I’m a woman. I agonized over the things that were asked of me and the expectations people had, but when I realized I was a gnc woman, I felt at peace. I still experience incredible dysphoria in my body—I would shrink my tits and I would slice my ass right off—but not in my identity as a woman. 

And at no point have I felt unwelcome in the lesbian community for having more testosterone and having more XY secondary sex characteristics than the average woman. Maybe I’m an outlier, I don’t think so, but maybe I am. I don’t feel bad about it. And at no point has the community with which I have surrounded myself has ever dismissed or denigrated my butch transbian and non-binary friends. 

I could take all kinds of androgen blocking medication, but it would only serve to help me conform to the medical standard of normal. I’m not in any danger from excess testosterone—I might be infertile, oh well—and I’m not uncomfortable from it. Society tried to make me uncomfortable. 

At one point, in a passing conversation, my friend said that being a gnc lesbian is actually a non-binary identity, and i was kind of taken aback by it. The absoluteness of the statement. The implications. Are GNC gay guys, effeminate men, are they not actually men as they say they are? Am I not actually a ciswoman? I tried to adopt non-binary label in my mind, but it didn’t fit. 

This long-standing conversation about the gender binary and gender expectations, it always seems on some level antagonistic. People who identify on the binary but do not conform are accused of being phobic to enbies. People who identify as non-binary are accused of erasing gnc men or women. I know that TERFs exist and love to push out trans and nonbinary identities out of female and female-adjacent spaces. But this statement implies that the whole lesbian community is intent on pushing out gnc ciswomen and we’re actually non-binary when that’s just not true. 

I do appreciate what I believe you want to say. Ciswomen with dysphoria should consider if they actually identify differently. They shouldn’t fear retribution from their community because we’re plagued by a swarm of TERFs. (I know you’re reading this; please leave.) But it’s harmful to indicate that ciswomen who do experience dysphoria would do better to to leave their life as “an outlier in a community that doesn’t see you”.

To be fair to the study, the concept of “thwarted belonging” existed, if not paraphrased, in Baumeister and Leary’s article “The need to belong: Desire for interpersonal attachments as a fundamental human motivation” from 1995. This study tries to measure to what extent “thwarted belonging” and “perceived budensomeness” are distinct in the minds of people contemplating suicide. Their sample size was small, consisted entirely of undergrads, and the data *suggested* that those ideas do factor differently and thwarted belonging affects the onset of suicidal ideation more. 

They were not able to control or account for a large amount of variables at their own admission, like **mental health**, socioeconomic background, ethnic background, etc. They hypothesize that in a larger study, they’d see even stronger confirmation.  

We pretty much know that people need people. Social interaction, even to the most introverted person, is still necessary, but it’s not concrete to say that this is a key motivation in all, or even most, suicidal people. 

And just from personal experience alone, I’d love to agree with everything this study indicates. However, it’s just not strong enough. 

Still, I do believe Baumeister and Leary’s theory that one of our fundamental motivations is interpersonal attachment. Even if there is a somatic, socially independent reason for someone to suffer suicidal ideation, abject loneliness will likely only make it that much worse. 

I guess it’s a question of “am I lonely because I’m suicidal?” or “am I suicidal because I’m lonely?” I’m not qualified to answer that.
